subject: Economics · Class 11 · Indian Economic Development
title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
source: NCERT Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 1 (Reprint 2026-27)

reels.title: Why 1947 still matters

scenes.sub: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
scenes.say: Why does a book about India's modern economy start before 1947? Because today's economy has its roots in almost two centuries of British rule. Let's see what India looked like on 15 August 1947.

scenes.text: India is the pivot of our Empire... if we lose India, the sun of our Empire will have set.
scenes.by: Victor Alexander Bruce (Lord Elgin), Viceroy of British India, 1894
scenes.say: In 1894, Viceroy Victor Alexander Bruce, also known as Lord Elgin, said India was the pivot of the British Empire. Lose India, and the sun sets on the Empire. Why was India so valuable? The answer is economics.

scenes.heading: The colonial deal
steps: Finished goods sold back to India
scenes.say: NCERT says the sole purpose of colonial rule was to reduce India to a raw material supplier for Britain's rapidly expanding industries. Colonial policies also turned India into a consumer of Britain's finished goods. So the gains flowed one way, and the profits stayed in Britain. Remember this two-way trap. It explains almost everything in this chapter.

scenes.heading: This chapter answers

items.text: What did India's economy look like in 1947?
Why did it stay underdeveloped and stagnant?
Which problems shaped planning after independence?

scenes.say: So we'll answer three questions. What did the economy look like in 1947? Why did it stagnate? And which problems shaped the strategy India chose after independence?

reels.beyond: Economic historian Angus Maddison estimated that India produced roughly a quarter of world output around 1700, but only about 4 percent by 1950. Such long-run estimates are debated, but they show the scale of relative decline. For the economic cost of Partition, NCERT points to Dr Rajendra Prasad's book 'India Divided'.
reels.examAngle: Answers in ESI (Economic and Social Issues, an RBI Grade B Phase 2 paper) on the structural problems of the Indian economy usually open with the colonial legacy. This chapter is your opening paragraph. Learn NCERT's 'sole purpose' line word for word.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, the main aim of British economic policy in India was to:
options: Make India a raw-material supplier and a market for British goods
quiz.why: Colonial policy protected Britain's interests: India supplied raw materials to British industry and bought its finished goods.

cards.q: What two roles did colonial policy force on India?
cards.a: Supplier of raw materials to British industry, and a consumer market for finished British goods.

cards.q: Roughly how long did British rule over India last?
cards.a: Almost two centuries, ending with independence on 15 August 1947.

cards.q: Complete NCERT's line: the sole purpose of British colonial rule in India was to…
cards.a: …reduce the country to a raw material supplier for Great Britain's rapidly expanding modern industrial base.

cards.q: Who called India 'the pivot of our Empire' in 1894?
cards.a: Viceroy Victor Alexander Bruce (Lord Elgin). NCERT prints the name as 'Vruce'.

reels.title: Before the British: a manufacturing hub

scenes.big: India used to export finished goods.
scenes.sub: An independent economy before British rule
scenes.say: Here's something people often forget. Before the British arrived, India had an independent economy, and it was famous around the world for things it made.

scenes.heading: Pre-British economy

items.text: Agriculture was the main livelihood...
...but there were many kinds of manufacturing too
Handicrafts: cotton and silk textiles, metal work, precious stone work
Sold worldwide for fine materials and high craftsmanship

scenes.say: Agriculture was the main source of livelihood, but the economy also had many kinds of manufacturing. Indian handicrafts, like cotton and silk textiles, metal work and precious stone work, had a worldwide market thanks to their quality and craftsmanship.

The star example is muslin from Dhaka, then spelled Dacca, now the capital of Bangladesh. Its finest variety was called malmal. Foreign travellers called it malmal shahi or malmal khas, meaning cloth fit for royalty.
scenes.heading: Box 1.1: Dhaka muslin

items.text: Muslin: a cotton textile from Bengal, around Dhaka (then 'Dacca')
'Daccai Muslin' gained worldwide fame
Its finest variety was called malmal
Also 'malmal shahi' or 'malmal khas': worn by, or fit for, the royalty

scenes.heading: What changed
scenes.say: Compare the before and after. India went from exporting fine finished goods to exporting raw materials, and its skilled artisans lost their markets. That reversal is the story of this chapter.

reels.beyond: There's a popular legend that a whole Dhaka muslin saree was fine enough to pass through a finger ring. Whether or not it's literally true, the legend shows how valuable this cloth was.
reels.examAngle: MCQs like to test names from the boxes: Dhaka muslin, malmal, malmal shahi, malmal khas.

quiz.q: According to NCERT (Box 1.1), the finest variety of Dhaka muslin was called:
quiz.why: NCERT Box 1.1: the finest muslin was 'malmal', also called 'malmal shahi' or 'malmal khas'.

cards.q: Name three handicraft industries India was famous for before British rule.
cards.a: Cotton and silk textiles, metal work, and precious stone work.

cards.q: What did 'malmal shahi' or 'malmal khas' mean?
cards.a: The finest Dhaka muslin, cloth fit for royalty.

reels.title: How rich was colonial India?

scenes.big: No sincere attempt to measure India's income.
scenes.sub: The colonial government never seriously estimated it
scenes.say: How rich was colonial India? Surprisingly, the colonial government never made a sincere attempt to measure India's national or per capita income.

scenes.heading: First, two terms (general definitions)

items.text: National income: value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year
Per capita income: national income ÷ population
Example: ₹100 crore income ÷ 10 crore people = ₹10 per person

scenes.say: Two terms first. National income is the value of all the final goods and services a country produces in a year. Per capita income is national income divided by the population, so it's the average person's share. If a country earns 100 crore rupees and has 10 crore people, per capita income is 10 rupees.

scenes.heading: Who estimated it?

items.text: Dadabhai Naoroji
William Digby
Findlay Shirras
V.K.R.V. Rao (the most significant estimates)
R.C. Desai

scenes.say: Some individuals tried, and their results were conflicting and inconsistent. The notable estimators were Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V K R V Rao and R C Desai. Rao's estimates were considered very significant. Memory trick: No Dog Should Run Desperately. Naoroji, Digby, Shirras, Rao, Desai.

scenes.label: yearly growth of total real output, first half of the 20th century

compare.label: yearly growth of output per person

scenes.say: Most studies agree that in the first half of the twentieth century, total real output grew less than 2 percent a year, and output per person only about half a percent. Using the rule of 70, which goes beyond the book, at half a percent a year it takes roughly 140 years for incomes to double.

reels.beyond: Rule of 70: divide 70 by the growth rate to get the doubling time. At 0.5% per capita growth, incomes double in about 140 years. At the 6–8% GDP growth India has seen in recent years, the economy doubles in roughly 9–12 years.
reels.examAngle: A classic factual MCQ asks whose colonial-era estimates were considered most significant. The answer is V.K.R.V. Rao.

quiz.q: Whose estimates of national income during the colonial period were considered very significant?
quiz.why: NCERT names five estimators but singles out V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates as very significant.

cards.q: Name the five notable estimators of India's colonial national income.
cards.a: Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao, R.C. Desai (mnemonic: No Dog Should Run Desperately).

cards.q: Growth of aggregate vs per capita output in the first half of the 20th century?
cards.a: Aggregate real output: under 2% a year. Per capita output: about 0.5% a year.

cards.q: Define per capita income.
cards.a: National income divided by the population, i.e. the average income per person.

reels.title: Agriculture: 85% of people, stuck in place

scenes.label: of Indians lived in villages and depended on agriculture
scenes.say: Under British rule, India's economy stayed fundamentally agrarian. About 85 percent of the population lived in villages and depended on agriculture, directly or indirectly.

scenes.text: The knowledge I have acquired of Bengal in two visits inclines me to believe that it is richer than Egypt.
scenes.say: Now picture Bengal in the seventeenth century. The French traveller Bernier wrote that it was richer than Egypt, with an abundance of cotton, silk, rice, sugar and butter. Keep that image and compare it with the stagnation two hundred years later.

scenes.heading: Stagnation, explained

items.text: Stagnation, and not infrequently unusual deterioration
Agricultural productivity was low
Output grew a little only because more land was farmed
No investment in terracing, flood control, drainage or desalinisation of soil

scenes.say: NCERT describes stagnation and, not infrequently, unusual deterioration. Here's the subtle point. Total farm output grew slightly, but only because more land was brought under cultivation, not because each acre produced more. Productivity stayed low, and there was almost no investment in terracing, flood control, drainage, or removing salt from soil.

scenes.heading: Why did it happen?

items.text: Land settlement systems, especially zamindari
Low levels of technology
Lack of irrigation facilities
Negligible use of fertilisers

scenes.say: NCERT says the stagnation was caused mainly by the land settlement systems the British introduced. On top of that came low technology, poor irrigation and almost no fertiliser use. We'll unpack the land systems in the next reel.

reels.beyond: Productivity means output per unit of input, such as tonnes of rice per hectare. A rise in total output with flat productivity is like a shop earning more only by opening more branches while each branch stays just as weak.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q3 asks for the main causes of agricultural stagnation. List: land settlement systems, zamindars' rent focus, revenue terms, low technology, poor irrigation, negligible fertilisers.

quiz.q: Despite stagnation, India's total agricultural output grew slightly under British rule mainly because of:
options: Expansion of the area under cultivation
quiz.why: Productivity stayed low. Growth came from expanding the area under cultivation.

cards.q: What share of India's population depended on agriculture under British rule?
cards.a: About 85% lived in villages and depended on agriculture directly or indirectly.

cards.q: What does NCERT call the main cause of agricultural stagnation?
cards.a: The land settlement systems introduced by the colonial government (especially zamindari).

cards.q: List four causes of low agricultural productivity in colonial India.
cards.a: Land settlement systems, low technology, lack of irrigation, negligible fertiliser use (plus no investment in terracing, flood control, drainage).

cards.q: Which two words does NCERT use for the condition of colonial agriculture?
cards.a: Stagnation and (not infrequently, unusual) deterioration.

reels.title: Zamindari: who took the harvest?

scenes.big: The farmer grew the crop. Someone else took the profit.
scenes.say: Imagine farming land all year, only for most of the profit to go to someone else. That was life under the zamindari system in the Bengal Presidency, which covered parts of today's eastern states.

scenes.heading: How zamindari worked
steps: Zamindar pays a fixed revenue to the British on fixed dates
Miss the date and the zamindar loses his rights
scenes.say: The chain worked like this. The cultivator grows the crop. The zamindar collects rent from him. The zamindar must deposit a fixed sum of revenue with the British by fixed dates, and if he fails, he loses his rights. So zamindars squeezed farmers as hard as they could.

scenes.heading: The result

items.text: Profit went to zamindars, not cultivators
Zamindars' only interest was collecting rent
Immense misery and social tension among cultivators
Many zamindars, and not just the government, did nothing to improve agriculture

scenes.say: The results: profits went to zamindars instead of cultivators. The zamindars' main interest was collecting rent, whatever condition the farmers were in. This caused immense misery and social tension. And NCERT notes that a considerable number of zamindars, not just the colonial government, did nothing to improve agriculture.

scenes.heading: Three land revenue systems

items.text: Zamindari under the Permanent Settlement: 1793, Lord Cornwallis; Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. A zamindar is the intermediary.
Ryotwari: associated with Thomas Munro in Madras, later also Bombay. The farmer (ryot) pays the state directly.
Mahalwari: 1822 (Holt Mackenzie); North-Western Provinces and Punjab. The village (mahal) pays as a unit.

scenes.say: Beyond NCERT, the British used three main revenue systems. Zamindari under the Permanent Settlement began in 1793 under Lord Cornwallis, in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, with the zamindar as the middleman. Ryotwari, associated with Thomas Munro in Madras and later used in Bombay, had the farmer pay the state directly. Under Mahalwari, from 1822 in the north-west, the whole village paid as one unit.

reels.beyond: After independence, land reforms set out to abolish intermediaries like zamindars. You'll meet this in the next chapter on 1950–90 policies. NCERT even asks whether zamindari has really been abolished.
reels.examAngle: Descriptive questions often ask you to link land tenure to farm productivity. Use the chain: fixed revenue → rent extraction → no investment → stagnation.

quiz.q: Why did zamindars squeeze cultivators for rent, according to NCERT?
options: The British paid zamindars a share of the crop
Revenue had to be deposited by fixed dates, or zamindars lost their rights
Cultivators owned the land and zamindars wanted it
quiz.why: The terms of the revenue settlement fixed the dates and sums. Failing to pay meant losing zamindari rights.

cards.q: In the zamindari system, who got the profit from agriculture?
cards.a: The zamindars, not the cultivators.

cards.q: How did the terms of revenue settlement make zamindars harsh?
cards.a: Fixed sums had to be deposited by fixed dates; failing that, zamindars lost their rights, so they extracted maximum rent.

cards.q: Ryotwari vs Zamindari vs Mahalwari: who paid revenue to the state?
cards.a: Ryotwari: the farmer directly. Zamindari: the zamindar (intermediary). Mahalwari: the village community as a unit.

cards.q: Which two books does NCERT suggest for studying colonial land settlements?
cards.a: R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' and B.H. Baden-Powell's 'The Land Systems of British India'. (Don't confuse R.C. Dutt with R.C. Desai, the income estimator.)

reels.title: Cash crops boomed. Farmers didn't.

scenes.sub: Growing crops to sell, not to eat
scenes.say: There was one bright spot. In some areas, cash crops gave relatively higher yields. This is called the commercialisation of agriculture: growing crops for the market instead of for your own family.

scenes.heading: Food crops vs cash crops

left.title: Food crops
items: Feed the family and the village

scenes.say: Food crops like rice and wheat feed families. Cash crops like cotton, jute and indigo are grown to sell, and under colonial rule they ultimately fed British factories.

scenes.heading: Why farmers didn't gain

items.text: Cash crops went to British industries back home
Only a small section of farmers switched crops
Tenants, small farmers and sharecroppers lacked resources, technology and incentive

scenes.say: Farmers' condition hardly improved, because the crops were used by British industries. Only a small section of farmers switched to commercial crops. A large section of tenants, small farmers and sharecroppers had no resources, no technology, and no incentive to invest.

scenes.heading: The hidden cost
steps: Railways carry cash crops to the ports
scenes.say: There was a hidden cost too. Railways linked the countryside to the ports and helped commercialisation spread. NCERT says this hurt the self-sufficiency of India's village economies, which had once produced most of what they needed.

reels.beyond: Indigo shows the dark side. In Champaran, Bihar, farmers were forced to grow indigo on part of their land (the tinkathia system). In 1917 this led to Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
reels.examAngle: If asked whether commercialisation helped Indian farmers: higher yields in some areas, but benefits went to British industry, and small farmers couldn't participate.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, which group could NOT benefit from the shift to commercial crops?
quiz.why: They had neither the resources, the technology nor the incentive to invest in agriculture.

cards.q: What is commercialisation of agriculture?
cards.a: A shift from growing food crops for one's own use to growing cash crops for sale in the market.

cards.q: Why didn't commercialisation improve farmers' condition under British rule?
cards.a: Cash crops ultimately served British industries; only a few farmers could switch; tenants, small farmers and sharecroppers lacked resources, technology and incentive.

reels.title: De-industrialisation: the two-fold motive

scenes.big: Old industries died. New ones weren't allowed to take their place.
scenes.say: India's world-famous handicrafts declined, and no modern industrial base was allowed to replace them. NCERT calls this the systematic de-industrialisation of India.

scenes.heading: The two-fold motive

items.text: Reduce India to an exporter of raw materials for Britain's modern industries
Turn India into a sprawling market for Britain's finished products

scenes.say: The colonial government had a two-fold motive. First, reduce India to an exporter of important raw materials for Britain's new industries. Second, turn India into a huge market for the finished products of those industries, so they could keep expanding to Britain's advantage.

scenes.heading: The chain reaction
steps: Cheap British imports fill the demand
scenes.say: Watch the chain reaction. Handicrafts decline, artisans lose their jobs, and locally made goods disappear from the market. That gap was profitably filled by cheap manufactured imports from Britain. Britain won on both ends.

reels.beyond: This is the economics behind the Swadeshi movement (1905) and Gandhi's charkha. Boycotting British cloth and spinning khadi were direct answers to de-industrialisation.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q5 is exactly this: the two-fold motive. Write both points, then add the result: unemployment plus new demand met by British imports.

quiz.q: Which of these was part of the two-fold motive behind de-industrialising India?
options: Making India a market for Britain's finished goods
Reducing India's exports of raw materials
quiz.why: The two motives: make India a raw-material exporter, and make India a market for British finished goods.

cards.q: What was the two-fold motive behind the systematic de-industrialisation of India?
cards.a: (1) Make India an exporter of raw materials for British industries; (2) make India a big market for British finished goods.

cards.q: What were two effects of the decline of Indian handicrafts?
cards.a: Massive unemployment among artisans, and a new demand for goods that was met by cheap British imports.

reels.title: Modern industry arrives, slowly

scenes.big: Second half of the 1800s: the first factories
scenes.sub: Modern industry took root, but grew very slowly
scenes.say: In the second half of the nineteenth century, modern industry began to take root in India. But it grew very slowly.

scenes.heading: The first mills
scenes.say: It started with two industries. Cotton textile mills were mainly owned by Indians and located in the west, in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Jute mills were dominated by foreigners and concentrated in Bengal. Easy way to remember: cotton, west, Indian. Jute, east, foreign.

scenes.heading: Milestones

events.text: Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) incorporated
Tata Airlines starts the aviation sector
Sugar, cement and paper industries come up

scenes.say: Here are the milestones in order. Cotton and jute mills came first, in the second half of the nineteenth century. Iron and steel began in the early twentieth century, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company, TISCO, was incorporated in 1907. Tata Airlines, a division of Tata and Sons, was set up in 1932. A few industries like sugar, cement and paper came up after the Second World War.

scenes.heading: Why Jamshedpur for TISCO?

items.text: Close to iron ore and coal deposits
Water from the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers
Rail link to markets and ports

scenes.say: NCERT asks why TISCO was set up at Jamshedpur, in today's Jharkhand. Steel needs iron ore and coal, which were nearby. It needs lots of water, which came from the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers. And it needs transport, which the railway provided.

reels.beyond: The aviation sector began on 15 October 1932, when J.R.D. Tata flew a mail plane from Karachi to Bombay for Tata Sons' new air service (NCERT calls it Tata Airlines). It was renamed Tata Air Lines in 1938 and became Air India in 1946.
reels.examAngle: Popular MCQs: TISCO's year (1907), Tata Airlines (1932), and who owned which mills (cotton: Indians, west; jute: foreigners, Bengal).

quiz.q: In colonial India, jute mills were:
options: Dominated by foreigners, concentrated in Bengal
quiz.why: Cotton mills: mainly Indian, in western India. Jute mills: dominated by foreigners, in Bengal.

cards.q: Cotton vs jute mills in colonial India: who owned them and where were they?
cards.a: Cotton: mainly Indian-owned, western India (Maharashtra, Gujarat). Jute: foreign-dominated, Bengal.

cards.q: When was TISCO incorporated?
Which industries came up after the Second World War?
cards.a: A few industries such as sugar, cement and paper.

reels.title: Missing: machines that make machines

scenes.big: Factories, yes. Machine-making industry, hardly any.
scenes.say: India now had some factories. But there was hardly any capital goods industry, and that was a serious problem.

scenes.heading: Know the difference
scenes.say: Capital goods industries make machine tools, which are then used to produce goods for everyday consumption. A cloth mill makes consumer goods. A factory that makes the looms for that cloth mill makes capital goods. Without capital goods, every new factory depends on imported machines.

scenes.heading: Other weaknesses of colonial industry

items.text: Could not replace the displaced handicraft industries
Low growth rate, small share of GDP / Gross Value Added
Public sector limited to railways, power, communications, ports and a few departmental undertakings

scenes.say: There were other weaknesses too. A few new factories could not replace the near-wholesale loss of traditional handicrafts. The industrial sector's growth rate stayed very small, and so did its share of GDP, the total value of everything produced in the country, also measured as Gross Value Added. And the public sector only operated in railways, power generation, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

reels.beyond: This gap explains a big policy choice after 1947. The Second Five Year Plan (1956), based on the Mahalanobis model, put heavy industry and capital goods at its centre.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q8: critically appraise the industrial policy. Cover no capital goods base, slow growth and low GDP share, handicrafts not replaced, and a very limited public sector.

quiz.q: Which of these is a capital good?
options: A shirt bought by a household
A machine tool used in a textile mill
quiz.why: Capital goods are used to produce other goods. A machine tool in a mill produces cloth.

cards.q: What is a capital goods industry?
cards.a: An industry that produces machine tools, which are in turn used to produce articles for current consumption.

cards.q: Where did the colonial public sector operate?
cards.a: Only in railways, power generation, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

reels.title: Foreign trade: a lopsided deal

scenes.big: An ancient trading nation, forced into lopsided trade.
scenes.sub: Structure, composition and volume all changed
scenes.say: India had been an important trading nation since ancient times. But colonial policies on production, trade and tariffs changed the structure, composition and volume of its foreign trade.

scenes.heading: What India traded

right.title: Imports: finished goods
items: Capital goods like light machinery from Britain

scenes.say: India became an exporter of primary products like raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute. It imported finished consumer goods, like cotton, silk and woollen clothes, and capital goods such as light machinery made in British factories.

scenes.label: of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain
scenes.say: Britain kept monopoly control over India's exports and imports. More than half of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain. The rest was allowed with a few countries like China, Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, and Persia, now Iran.

scenes.heading: The Suez Canal, 1869
steps: Joins the Mediterranean (Port Said) to the Red Sea (Gulf of Suez)
Britain's grip on India's trade tightens
scenes.say: Then in 1869 the Suez Canal opened. It's an artificial waterway in Egypt joining the Mediterranean Sea at Port Said with the Gulf of Suez on the Red Sea. Ships no longer had to sail around Africa, transport became cheaper, and Britain's access to the Indian market got easier. Its control over India's trade grew even stronger.

reels.beyond: Today the pattern has flipped. India's largest export categories include engineering goods, refined petroleum products and pharmaceuticals, and its trade partners are spread worldwide. The Economic Survey, published every year by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, is the standard source for these trade figures.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q15 asks for the volume and direction of trade. Volume: a large export surplus, which came at a huge cost and was drained away (next reel). Direction: more than 50% with Britain. Composition: primary products out, finished goods in.

quiz.q: The opening of the Suez Canal (1869) affected India's trade by:
options: Ending British control over India's trade
Making access to the Indian market easier and intensifying British control
quiz.why: It cut transport costs and made the Indian market easier to reach, which intensified British control.

cards.q: What was the composition of India's colonial trade?
cards.a: Exports: primary products (raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute). Imports: finished consumer goods and light machinery from Britain.

cards.q: How much of India's foreign trade went to Britain, and who else was allowed?
cards.a: More than half; the rest with countries like China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Persia (Iran).

cards.q: Suez Canal: which year and which seas does it link?
cards.a: Opened 1869; links the Mediterranean (Port Said) with the Red Sea (Gulf of Suez).

cards.q: What characterised the volume of India's colonial foreign trade?
cards.a: A large export surplus, which came at a huge cost to the economy and was drained away.

reels.title: Export surplus & the drain of wealth

scenes.big: India exported more than it imported. So why did it get poorer?
scenes.sub: The paradox of the export surplus
scenes.say: Here's a puzzle. Throughout the colonial period, India had a large export surplus. It sold more than it bought. Normally that would make a country richer. So why did India get poorer?

scenes.heading: The catch

items.text: Food grains, clothes and kerosene were scarcely available at home
The surplus brought no gold or silver into India

scenes.say: First, the surplus came at a huge cost. Essential goods like food grains, clothes and kerosene were scarcely available in India's own markets. Second, the surplus did not bring any gold or silver into the country.

scenes.heading: Where the surplus went
steps: Expenses of the colonial office in Britain
Imports of invisible items (e.g. shipping, insurance)
scenes.say: So where did the money go? It paid for the expenses of an office the colonial government ran in Britain, for wars fought by the British government, and for imports of invisible items, like shipping and insurance services. Together, this is called the drain of Indian wealth.

Beyond NCERT, the person most associated with this idea is Dadabhai Naoroji, the same man who estimated national income. In his book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, he argued that India's wealth was being drained to Britain through home charges like officials' salaries and pensions, interest on debt, and military costs.
scenes.heading: Naoroji's Drain Theory

items.text: Dadabhai Naoroji, 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901)
India's wealth flowed to Britain through 'Home Charges'
Salaries and pensions of British officials, interest on debt, military costs

reels.beyond: Invisibles are the non-goods part of trade. In India's current account today, 'invisibles' cover services (like shipping, insurance, banking and software), transfers such as remittances, and income such as interest and dividends. You'll study them in RBI's balance-of-payments topics.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q9: 'What do you understand by the drain of Indian wealth?' Cover the export surplus, no gold or silver inflow, and the money paying for the British office, wars and invisible imports. Naoroji's name is a bonus.

quiz.q: India's colonial export surplus was mainly used to:
options: Import gold and silver into India
Pay for the British colonial office, wars and invisible imports
quiz.why: It brought no gold or silver. It paid for the colonial office in Britain, British wars and invisible imports, which is the drain of wealth.

cards.q: What was the 'drain of Indian wealth'?
cards.a: India's export surplus brought no gold/silver; it paid for the colonial office in Britain, British wars and invisible imports, so wealth flowed out of India.

cards.q: Who is associated with the Drain Theory and in which book?
cards.a: Dadabhai Naoroji, 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901).

cards.q: What cost did India pay for its export surplus at home?
cards.a: Essentials like food grains, clothes and kerosene were scarcely available in the domestic market.

reels.title: 1881 census & the demographic transition

scenes.say: Detailed information about British India's population was first collected in the census of 1881. It had limitations, but it showed how unevenly India's population was growing. After that, a census was held every ten years.

scenes.heading: Demographic transition, simply

items.text: Stage 1: high birth rate + high death rate → slow growth
Stage 2: death rate falls, birth rate stays high → population grows fast

scenes.say: Demographic transition describes how population changes as a country develops. In stage one, both birth and death rates are high, so population grows slowly. In stage two, better health and food cut the death rate, but the birth rate stays high, so population grows fast.

scenes.heading: India's transition
scenes.say: India was in the first stage before 1921. The second stage began after 1921. At this point, neither India's total population nor its growth rate was very high.

reels.beyond: 1921 is often called the 'Year of the Great Divide' in Indian demography. Before it, population rose and fell with famines and epidemics. After it, population grew continuously. One more detail: a first, non-synchronous count was taken in 1872, but 1881 was the first regular, synchronous census. For NCERT-based questions, answer 1881.
reels.examAngle: Two easy marks: the first census (1881) and the year that divides the first and second stages (1921). Exercise Q10 and Q14 ask exactly these.

quiz.q: Which year marks India's move from the first to the second stage of demographic transition?
quiz.why: Before 1921 India was in the first stage. The second stage began after 1921.

cards.q: When was the first census of British India held?
cards.a: 1881 (and every ten years after that).

cards.q: Which year divides the first and second stages of India's demographic transition?
cards.a: 1921 (the 'Year of the Great Divide').

cards.q: What happens in the second stage of demographic transition?
cards.a: Death rate falls while birth rate stays high, so population grows rapidly.

reels.title: Health & literacy at independence

scenes.label: life expectancy in colonial India (around independence)
scenes.say: Life expectancy was very low: about 32 years, compared with about 70 years today.

scenes.label: infant deaths per 1,000 live births (IMR), colonial India
scenes.say: The infant mortality rate measures how many babies die before their first birthday for every thousand born alive. At independence it was about 218, so more than one in five babies didn't survive their first year. NCERT gives the present figure as 28.

scenes.heading: Literacy then
scenes.say: Literacy was also low. Overall literacy was below 16 percent, and female literacy was a negligible 7 percent or so.

scenes.heading: Why so grim?

items.text: Public health facilities unavailable or highly inadequate
Water-borne and air-borne diseases were rampant
Very high overall mortality rate
Frequent natural calamities and famines pauperised people
Extensive poverty (no reliable data, but clearly widespread)

scenes.say: The reasons: public health facilities were either unavailable or highly inadequate, so water-borne and air-borne diseases were rampant and the death rate was very high. Frequent natural calamities and famines pushed people deeper into poverty. There's no reliable data on poverty from that time, but extensive poverty clearly existed.

reels.beyond: The Bengal Famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2–3 million people. Amartya Sen's 'Poverty and Famines' argued that famines are often about people losing the ability to buy or access food (their 'entitlements'), not only about too little food. The 2011 Census put literacy at about 74% (female about 65%).
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q11 asks for a quantitative appraisal of the demographic profile. Quote the numbers: literacy under 16% (female about 7%), IMR 218 per 1,000, life expectancy 32 years.

quiz.q: In colonial India, around the time of independence, the infant mortality rate was about:
quiz.why: NCERT gives about 218 per thousand at the time, compared with 28 today.

cards.q: Give the four key social indicators of colonial India (NCERT).
cards.a: Literacy under 16%, female literacy about 7%, infant mortality about 218 per 1,000, life expectancy about 32 years.

cards.q: What is the infant mortality rate (IMR)?
cards.a: The number of infants who die before their first birthday per 1,000 live births.

cards.q: Why was mortality so high in colonial India?
cards.a: Inadequate or unavailable public health facilities, rampant water- and air-borne diseases, frequent natural calamities and famines, and extensive poverty.

reels.title: Where people worked

scenes.big: Occupational structure: who works in which sector
scenes.sub: In colonial India it barely changed
scenes.say: Occupational structure means how a country's workers are spread across sectors like agriculture, manufacturing and services. In colonial India it showed little sign of change.

scenes.heading: Share of the workforce
scenes.say: Agriculture employed the largest share, about 70 to 75 percent of the workforce. Manufacturing employed only about 10 percent, and services about 15 to 20 percent.

scenes.heading: Growing regional variation

left.title: Less dependent on farming
items: Madras Presidency (today's Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka)

scenes.say: There was growing regional variation. In the Madras Presidency, which covered today's Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka, and in Bombay and Bengal, dependence on agriculture fell while manufacturing and services grew. In Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab, agriculture's share of the workforce actually rose.

scenes.label: of India's workers are still in agriculture (PLFS 2023–24, approx.)
scenes.say: Beyond NCERT: even today, government survey data shows roughly 46 percent of India's workers in agriculture. It's the largest employer, though its share of GDP is far smaller. That structural problem has colonial roots.

reels.beyond: Economists expect workers to move from agriculture to industry and services as a country develops. India's path has been unusual: services grew faster than manufacturing, and agriculture still holds a large share of jobs.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q12: list the sector shares (70–75 / 10 / 15–20) and the regional variation, naming the regions on both sides.

quiz.q: In which regions did the share of the workforce in agriculture INCREASE during the colonial period?
quiz.why: Madras, Bombay and Bengal moved away from agriculture. Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab became more dependent on it.

cards.q: Colonial India's occupational structure: share of agriculture, manufacturing, services?
cards.a: Agriculture 70–75%, manufacturing about 10%, services 15–20%.

cards.q: Which regions saw falling dependence on agriculture, and which saw rising dependence?
cards.a: Falling: Madras Presidency, Bombay, Bengal. Rising: Orissa, Rajasthan, Punjab.

reels.title: Railways: a double-edged track

scenes.big: Britain's biggest 'gift', or a tool of empire?
scenes.say: The railways are often called one of Britain's most important contributions to India. Let's look at both edges of this track.

scenes.heading: Key dates

events.text: First passenger train: Bombay to Thane (beyond NCERT)
Photo in NCERT: the first railway bridge linking Bombay with Thane

scenes.say: NCERT says the British introduced railways in India in 1850, and its photo shows the first railway bridge linking Bombay with Thane, from 1854. Beyond the book, the first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853, from Bombay to Thane. For exams, remember 1850 from NCERT and 1853 for the first passenger train.

scenes.heading: Two effects

right.title: ⚠️ Negative
items: Hurt the self-sufficiency of village economies
Exports grew, but Indians rarely benefited

scenes.say: Railways affected the economy in two important ways. On one hand, people could travel long distances, which broke geographical and cultural barriers. On the other hand, railways fostered the commercialisation of agriculture, which hurt the self-sufficiency of village economies. Exports grew, but the benefits rarely reached Indians.

scenes.heading: The verdict

items.text: Real motive: serve colonial interests, not provide amenities
Social benefits were outweighed by the country's huge economic loss

scenes.say: NCERT's verdict: infrastructure was built mainly to serve colonial interests, not to provide basic amenities. The social benefits Indians got from the railways were outweighed by the country's huge economic loss.

reels.beyond: At independence, India's railway network was among the largest in the world, but it was designed to link the interior to the ports, not to connect Indian regions to each other.
reels.examAngle: A frequent 'discuss' question: were the railways a positive contribution? Give both effects, then NCERT's conclusion that the social benefits were outweighed by economic loss.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, how did railways hurt the Indian economy?
options: They fostered commercialisation of agriculture, hurting village self-sufficiency
They raised India's import of raw materials
quiz.why: Commercialisation of agriculture weakened the self-sufficiency of village economies, and the benefits of rising exports rarely reached Indians.

cards.q: When did NCERT say railways were introduced in India? When did the first passenger train run?
cards.a: Introduced in 1850 (NCERT); first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853, Bombay to Thane.

cards.q: What were the two important effects of railways on the Indian economy?
cards.a: (1) Long-distance travel broke geographical and cultural barriers; (2) they fostered commercialisation of agriculture, hurting village self-sufficiency.

reels.title: Roads, canals, telegraph & post

scenes.big: Built for the Empire, not for the people.
scenes.say: Railways, ports, water transport, post and telegraph all developed under colonial rule. But the motive was to serve colonial interests, not to provide basic amenities.

scenes.heading: Why roads were built
steps: Carry raw materials to the railway station or port
Ship them to England and abroad
scenes.say: Roads built before the British weren't fit for modern transport. The new roads mainly served two purposes: moving the army within India, and carrying raw materials from the countryside to the nearest railway station or port, to be shipped to England.

scenes.heading: The gaps

items.text: Acute shortage of all-weather roads to rural areas
Villagers suffered during natural calamities and famines
Measures for inland trade and sea lanes: far from satisfactory
Coast Canal (Orissa): built at huge cost, lost to a parallel railway, then abandoned
Expensive electric telegraph: used to maintain law and order
Postal services: useful, but always inadequate

scenes.say: There was an acute shortage of all-weather roads into rural areas, so villagers suffered badly during natural calamities and famines. Measures for inland trade and sea lanes were, in NCERT's words, far from satisfactory. The Coast Canal on the Orissa coast was built at huge cost, couldn't compete with a railway running parallel to it, and was abandoned. The expensive electric telegraph served law and order. Postal services were useful but remained inadequate.

reels.beyond: Rural road connectivity stayed a policy priority long after independence. A national programme for all-weather rural roads, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, was launched in 2000.
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q7: the objectives behind colonial infrastructure. The answer is colonial interests: moving the army, moving raw materials to ports, and law and order through the telegraph.

quiz.q: The Coast Canal on the Orissa coast was abandoned because:
options: It was destroyed in a cyclone
It could not compete with a railway running parallel to it
The British moved trade to the Suez Canal
It was too small for ships
quiz.why: It was built at huge cost to the exchequer, but the parallel railway was more competitive, so it was abandoned.

cards.q: What were the main purposes of roads built under British rule?
cards.a: Moving the army within India, and moving raw materials to railway stations and ports for export.

cards.q: What was the purpose of the electric telegraph in colonial India?
cards.a: Maintaining law and order.

cards.q: What example does NCERT give of an uneconomical inland waterway?
cards.a: The Coast Canal on the Orissa coast, abandoned after failing to compete with a parallel railway.

reels.title: 1947 balance sheet: the challenges ahead

scenes.say: By independence, two centuries of colonial rule had left a mark on every part of the economy. Here's the to-do list the new government inherited.

scenes.heading: The challenges

items.text: Agriculture: surplus labour, extremely low productivity
Industry: needed modernisation, diversification, capacity building, public investment
Trade: oriented to feed Britain's Industrial Revolution
Infrastructure: needed upgrading, expansion and public orientation
Poverty and unemployment: needed welfare-oriented policy

scenes.say: Agriculture had surplus labour and extremely low productivity. Industry needed modernisation, diversification, capacity building and more public investment. Foreign trade had been oriented to feed Britain's Industrial Revolution. Infrastructure, even the famous railways, needed upgrading, expansion and a public orientation. And rampant poverty and unemployment called for welfare-oriented public policy.

scenes.heading: Debate: was the Raj good for India?
scenes.say: NCERT asks you to debate whether British rule was good for India. On one side: railways, ports, the telegraph, some modern industry and the census. On the other: the drain of wealth, de-industrialisation, agricultural stagnation, famines, and per capita growth of about half a percent. NCERT concludes that the efforts were spiced with selfish motives, and independent India had to build on this base through planning.

scenes.heading: What came next
steps: Need for a big public effort
scenes.say: Beyond this chapter: that's why independent India chose planned development. The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 and launched Five Year Plans to rebuild on this base. That's the next chapter.

reels.beyond: The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. Knowing the arc from colonial legacy to planning to reforms helps with descriptive answers in ESI (Economic and Social Issues).
reels.examAngle: Exercise Q13 and Q16. For 'positive contributions', give a balanced answer, then conclude with NCERT's line that the efforts were 'spiced with selfish motives'.

quiz.q: Which was NOT one of the challenges India faced at independence, according to NCERT?
options: Surplus labour and low productivity in agriculture
Industry needing modernisation and public investment
A large and well-developed capital goods sector to manage
quiz.why: India had hardly any capital goods industry. Building one was itself a challenge.

cards.q: List India's five big economic challenges at independence.
cards.a: Agriculture (surplus labour, low productivity), industry (modernise, diversify, public investment), trade (oriented to Britain), infrastructure (upgrade, expand), poverty and unemployment (welfare policy).

cards.q: How did NCERT conclude on Britain's infrastructure efforts?
cards.a: Some efforts were made, but they were 'spiced with selfish motives'; independent India had to build on this base through planning.
